speakeroldname: Mrs. Shirley Martin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity to speak on third reading of Bill C-118, an Act to amend the Customs Tariff. As Members will know, this Bill provides for the reduction and removal of duties on a narrow range of products not manufactured in Canada.
Bill C-118 also makes some technical amendments to the Customs Tariff to correct errors in the new harmonized system which came into effect on January 1, 1988, and to allow facsimile transmission equipment and diesel engines to continue to enter Canada at the rates which have historically been applied.
I would be remiss, Mr. Speaker, if I did not make mention of my colleagues on the finance committee who once again put their collective expertise to work to deal expeditiously with this piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take only a few minutes to add a brief word on behalf of the Liberal Party with regard to this Bill. Normally, of course, my distinguished colleague, the Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), would be responding on this Bill,
but this morning she is temporarily detained elsewhere here on Parliament Hill. Since she cannot be with us to address this issue I will make a few remarks on her behalf.
Bill C-118 is designed to do a number of things. It is to correct errors in the new harmonized system of tariffs by amending Section 20 to restore duty treatment for certain imported alcoholic beverages. It will correct an error in the new system in relation to remissions under the machinery program. It will delete the tariff item being amended in Schedule I to the Bill.
Another item in the Bill is the continued free entry for facsimile equipment not made in Canada. This equipment is commonly referred to as telecopying equipment. There will also be a removal of the duty on radio controlled model glider kits and radio controlled self-propelled electrically powered model vehicle kits. This hobby equipment is not manufactured in Canada and therefore the Tariff Board recommended that free entry be provided for these items. The Bill will address that issue as well.
Schedule II also provides for the removal of the duty on burial shrouds. We are told that they are not made in Canada and I suppose until such time as they are made here there would be no purpose in having a duty to protect an industry that does not exist at the present time.
There are a number of items generally involving tariffs which sometimes come to the attention of Members as being contentious. I remember a year or two ago a case involving veterinarians. Veterinarians working with farm animals have a specific piece of equipment which they attach to the back of their truck. This equipment has a refrigerated compartment in which to keep drugs and another space to keep medical equipment used by veterinarians. This piece of equipment had a duty imposed on it, even though it was not made in Canada.
A number of Members of Parliament, including myself, wrote to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to ask that he intervene with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) in order to have the duty removed since there was really no purpose for it. It only created hardship for some veterinarians. I am happy to say that the representation was effective because the Minister saw fit to intervene and I understand the duty was eventually removed. That is an example of how these tariffs are sometimes counterproductive.
I am told that officials at the Department of Customs and Excise interpreted that equipment to be a part of a truck body,

which it was not, and gave it the same recognition as a camper. Obviously it had nothing to do with camping but met a very specific purpose and should not have been subject to a tariff.
I want to bring to the attention of the House a letter I received concerning another tariff issue. Since we are dealing with an Act to amend the Customs Tariff Act, I thought I would use this opportunity to raise a specific tariff issue that has been brought to my attention by a textile firm in my constituency known as Consoltex. Consoltex is a company located in Montreal but which also has a plant in my constituency.

In the letter sent to me by Mr. John F. Trickett of Consoltex, he informed me of correspondence he had with the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) after the announcement on March 22, 1988 of the tariff reform for the textile and clothing industries.
So Mr. Trickett said in a letter that he sent to the Minister, and I quote:
I am very concerned that this list of fabrics included in Schedule I.. .
... of the tariff list...
... was not thoroughly considered and contains several items that are definitely manufactured in Canada by Consoltex as well as other textile companies. Furthermore, some products on this list can be directly substituted for others made in Canada.
It is essential that direct consultation with us and other Canadian textile companies take place before Finalizing what fabrics-will be eligible for customs exemption.
So in this case, Mr. Speaker, we have a situation where the Government has chosen this time, it seems, to eliminate tariffs which should not have been eliminated; that is, removing them will hurt the textile industry that is so important for the riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.
I will give you an example of some of these fabrics, according to the list provided by Consoltex:
(1) Fabrics of a weight not exceeding 70 grams per square meter, other than lining fabrics.
It seems this is one type of fabric for which we are proposing tariff remission. Consoltex informs us that they manufacture this product themselves.
(2)	Fabrics containing 35 per cent or more, by weight, of silk.
Consoltex says:
This item alone could result in unfair competition for virtually all fabrics now manufactured in Canada, because of the tariff remission.
In other words, this particular product that will not be subject to duty could be substituted for others that are now being manufactured in Canada.
(3)	Jacquard fabrics: These fabrics are now manufactured in Canada, and Consoltex is manufacturing more and more fabrics that are not included in this item but might be adversely affected by duty free imports under this tariff item.
(4)	"Leno" fabrics containing 50 per cent or more, by weight, of cotton.
Consoltex manufactures "Leno" fabrics and other fabrics that are not included in this item and would be directly affected and, in fact, replaced by duty-free imports.
Mr. Speaker, the rest of the text I have here reads as follows:
In addition to the above items, there are other products on the list that
require further clarification and definition. The list is too vague in its present
form, and significant improvements are urgently needed.
What Mr. Trickett is trying to say is this: Although all Members of this House do, I imagine, approve of the principle of tariff remission which is important to the garment manufacturers in my riding, we should not forget that those who manufacture fabrics in Canada must be protected, so that when we provide for tariff remission, we should make sure that we protect products that are manufactured in Canada or that can be replaced by a product manufactured in our own country.
Mr. Speaker, those were my brief comments this morning on Bill C-l 18, and I also wanted to take this opportunity to point out that one of the manufacturers in my riding is dissatisfied with some of this Government's tariff policies.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you, and we in the Liberal Party intend to co-operate in getting this Bill through the House as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, this is not one of the earthshaking pieces of legislation to come before the House of Commons. Nevertheless, it is legislation which, during the second reading debate, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Hawkes), suggested represented the following principle: "The policy of the Government is to meet the needs of the business sector and individuals by amending the tariffs in its annual Budget. This Bill maintains this tradition, and I therefore urge the House to adopt it as quickly as possible".
It is interesting in the context of that statement to recount to the House of Commons the case of a machine manufacturing plant in my constituency, Tri-Way Machine Ltd. which is one of the few companies in this country capable of producing a machining system, combined with transfer mechanisms within the machining system, all computerized, which permits a product to be produced to extremely high levels of tolerance. We raised the case of Tri-Way with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) this past year. In fact, Tri-Way officials came to Ottawa to point out very clearly to the Government the tremendous irony which exists in the present tariff schedule. It is the irony that if one imports certain machines which go to make up this transfer system of machining, one can import them at no tariff rate.
If, however, one imports a complete transfer system-with the machining and transfer mechanisms built in-one has to
April 22, 1988

pay a tariff of over 9 per cent. One could not recognize a more detrimental situation for the production of these very sophisticated high-tech machines here in Canada. By that structure of the tariff, every incentive is given to plants to bring into the country the basic machines and to assemble a transfer system based on those machines, instead of actually creating the transfer system from the ground up, as Tri-Way itself has done in Windsor, and it has employed over 200 people in the process of production.
This case was put very, very clearly to the Minister of National Revenue. It was put very clearly to the Minister of Finance. We have here a Bill which claims to represent amendments to the customs tariff in response to requests from the private sector. Yet there is absolutely no response to this request which would give to this country a greater capacity to produce sophisticated machinery right from the ground up, to expand employment and thereby build the base for exports in the future.
Tri-Way exports the great bulk of what it produces to other countries, mostly the United States. Yet the Government has seen fit to ignore completely this absolutely straightforward and legitimate request from this important company within my constituency for a tariff change . I think it is a shame the Government would act that way with respect to this specific company.
I think there is inherent in the changes proposed in this Bill a perspective on Canada for the future which reflects exactly that "no" to a high-tech machine- based company in my own constituency. The kinds of changes which are taking place with respect to this Bill, when you consider them in detail, indicate what we are opening ourselves up for. We are reducing the incentive to Canadian producers to produce high-technology machinery which is crucial for many sectors of our economy in the future.
If we take, for instance, the changes which have to do with machinery which is employed in mining, recovering and producing crude oil from shales, oil sands or tar sands, what do we see taking place? We see a vast variety of machines which we in this country have the capacity to produce and the incentives to produce them stripped away from the various tariffs which existed under the general preferential tariff or the most favoured nation tariff. We see a reduction to free entry for the whole set of these machines, including bridge conveyer systems, mechanical shovels, multi-bucket excavators, coke cutters and so on.
I cannot understand the logic of trying to paint a picture, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) sometimes does, of this country as a technologically sophisticated nation with a capacity, not just to produce this kind of important machinery but to export it, based on the fact that we have resource sectors here which require such machinery. I cannot see the logic of taking the incentives to Canadian producers to produce this machinery here in Canada out of our tariff structure.
Customs Tariff
If what the bulk of this Bill were aiming to do was to make some reductions on very skilled, non-technology intensive products, and to give some advantages to less developed countries to be able to export into our country, one would have no problem with that. It would make some sort of sense. But to take the very top, the most sophisticated of our products, the most sophisticated potential for the future of the country, as represented in some of this machinery which is being given duty-free status, as represented by the lack of response to a company such as Tri-Way, which is producing extremely sophisticated machining systems, is to say that the Government believes that the future of Canada is to be a resource producer. It is to say that our future is to be an extractor of raw materials rather than a high-tech producer able to compete with the rest of the world.
That just makes no sense from an industrial policy perspective whatsoever. Anyone who looks seriously at what our industrial future will be, in terms of what we can potentially compete in against the lower wage, lower benefit, developing countries of the world, comes to an obvious conclusion. We have to move toward more sophisticated production. We have to move toward production of precisely the type of items I am talking about, much more sophisticated technology machine goods. That is the direction we have to take. That is the direction which will make us competitive, because the capacity to export products which have a skill input is important for the future of Canada. Yet the Government heads us in precisely the opposite direction.
I grant Hon. Members that this is not, as I started out to say, a major Bill. However, taken together with the other elements which exist in the Government's trade policy direction, there is only one conclusion that one can draw. It is that the Government does not have a trade policy which sees Canada as a leader in high technology production in the future. Instead, it sees us tied in dependent terms to the United States through the trade agreement that it wishes to sign. It sees our companies as unable to respond rapidly and flexibly to trade threats, as Bill C-110 which we talked about yesterday demonstrates. It sees us as a country which is devoted to importing other people's machinery, to giving other people advantages and benefits, and to cutting out the incentives which exist for our country with respect to high technology machinery for the future.
It is a policy which is as ridiculous as one can possibly imagine. It is sending us on a track which in 20 years' time will make us much less competitive and much more dependent at a time when we could be taking steps, albeit small ones in this Bill, in the opposite direction. We could be taking steps which would give us much more capacity for sophisticated machinery production in the future, not just in the case of Tri-Way in my own constitutency but in the case of the various machine goods which are noted in this Bill itself.

Customs Tariff
Thus we have a Bill which is a failure through what it omits, such as the Tri-Way case and the tremendous benefits which machine transfer systems being produced from the ground up could give to the country. We have a Bill which is a failure in terms of what is in it, in terms of cutting away incentives which presently exist that favour us moving in the direction of higher technology and more sophisticated production which will give us a place in the world in the future.
If this were taking place at a time when we had prosperity throughout the country one might sit back and not be so concerned about it. However, if one looks at the statistics for Canada one sees that, with the exception of small geographic parts of the country, unemployment rates are unacceptably high. We see unemployment rates in Atlantic Canada which are simply shameful for us to accept. We see unemployment rates in the West where there is a lack of a diversified manufacturing base which western economists and western producers are very concerned about. We see in much of Ontario and Quebec communities which face serious problems for the future. We see textile communities, for instance-

... there are textile communities in Quebec that are facing a very uncertain future. We must try to do something about these problems, and I am referring to present and future jobs. Unfortunately, there is nothing in this Bill that shows the Government understands the problem.

The same is true of Ontario. In my own community of Windsor we have an unemployment rate of over 9 per cent. That is the official rate. Many people in the community think that the unofficial rate is much higher. In great parts of northern Ontario unemployment rates are as bad or worse. In Brantford, unemployment rates are at levels which reflect the tremendous collapse of one of our important machine producing sectors of the past, the farm equipment sector.
With the small exceptions of certain geographic areas, in this country we have serious economic problems and unemployment. This unemployment is the basic and fundamental reason why we should be looking at a future which gives us high technology potential and potential in the machining sector. These are the sectors where highly skilled employment is possible in the future. These are the sectors where exports based on these skills, growth of technology, and the sophistication of the products that can be produced in this country. That is where the future exists for Canada. Yet this Bill takes steps away from that future.
I have gone through the Tri-Way plant in Windsor and seen the tremendously sophisticated production of which it is capable. Officials of that plant have also put to me the fact that that production is vulnerable if there is not a fair base of protection for them, not to establish high costs for Canadians buying their equipment, but to establish fairness between those
who import the equipment and those who import the parts and assemble them here in Canada.
I would urge that the Government look at this Bill again, that it realize that it has embarked very much in the wrong direction, and that it give this country a sense of a high-tech future which this Bill does not present to us.

I have a question for the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon). I was not privileged to be in the House when the Government introduced the Bill, but I have gone through the remarks of the Hon. Member who introduced it on behalf of the Government. I did not see any explanation of the Bill, other than a very brief description of some of the goods on which the Government is proposing to reduce the tariffs.
Did the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor have an opportunity to look into the reasons for some of the tariff reductions that were posted? I notice that some of them include tariff item 73.08 which would reduce the tariff to zero on structures and parts of structures mostly for bridges and bridge sections, lock gates, towers, masts, roofing, framework, et cetera. In short, these are mostly products made out of steel in which we understood Canada normally has an ability to be quite competitive. Does the Hon. Member have any insight as to why these proposals were put forward in this case?
I notice that very large compressors will now be permitted to have better access from outside the country. I know these are very much in use in the oil and mining industries, and I wondered if the Hon. Member has any insight into the effect that this change will have on the steel industry which produces materials for doors, belts, and so on. What, if any, impact will there be on the compressor industry? I know that that industry is fairly important in Calgary and the West as they are great users of compressed air in the oil and mining industries.

The Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Hawkes) was absolutely frank in saying why these particular changes had been introduced. He said that the policy of the Government is to meet the needs of the business sector and individuals by amending the tariffs in its annual Budgets. The Bill maintains this tradition.
Unfortunately, that is not quite an accurate statement. The needs of businesses which have been put before the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance have not been met, except on a selective basis. There have been certain things on which the Government has stated that it would accept that representation and put it into effect. But, for example, on this representation from Tri-Way to get the capacity for better machining and better production of transfer systems in this country, the Government states that it will not select that particular suggestion.
The logic of saying to the business community that it will be responsive is not being followed with respect to this Bill. Therefore, one has to ask, why is the Government choosing
April 22, 1988

particular groups and individuals to say yes to, and other groups and other individuals to say no to?
I was particularly intrigued in trying to answer that question by the fact that burial shrouds were going to be allowed into the country duty free. Personally, Mr. Speaker, I associated that with the next election and the fact that there would be a tremendous demand on the part of the Conservative Party for such burial shrouds.
With respect to the points raised by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), there are serious problems raised. Here we are being hit by countervail tariffs in the United States on some of our specialty steel items, and what we do is to establish a reduction in tariff levels, and in many cases completely free entry for other specialty steel items coming into this country.
Again, we seem to be hurting an industry which has been tremendously competitive, which has a high technology base, and which has tremendous skill inputs. My friend asks, does it make sense? My answer is that I do not think it does make sense. I do not think there is logic in what has been put before us, and certainly that logic has not, at any stage, been presented by the Government in attempting to defend this unfortunate Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I hasten to congratulate the Hon. Member on his excellent speech about a Bill which, at first sight, is not of great moment in the context of more important legislation we will be considering to implement the free trade agreement. Nevertheless, he has indicated to us in a very informative way some of its implications.
What is involved here is the lowering of customs duties on goods coming into Canada. Part of the free trade agreement, of course, is to eliminate almost all tariffs over a period of time. That is intended to gain Canadian access to the American market. I think Canadians have done reasonably well over the last little while in the American market because of the value of the Canadian dollar compared to the American dollar. That difference, which was to our advantage, overcame some of the tariff barriers imposed by the Americans.
I am sure my colleague would be more than willing to examine the situation of Birla Industries in Windsor in the context of the free trade agreement and the increase in the value of our dollar. Perhaps he would also consider it in the context of the Canadian dollar achieving the not unprecedented level of 90 cents or even parity, and what would be the implications of that situation for Canadian industry, particularly in the City of Windsor, the representation of which I share with my colleague as a Member of Parliament.
Customs Tariff

Mr. Speaker, the collapse of Birla Industries is perhaps the sixth or seventh shut-down of an auto parts plant to hit Windsor and Essex County in the last year. Previous shut-downs include Cross-LaSalle, International Tools Ltd., and others.
There has been a constant and growing sense of pressure on the auto parts industry which comes from three things. First, because of a possible downturn in the industry associated with the problems of a lack of government policy and lack of enforcement of the 60 per cent Canadian content rule on Japanese producers. The second factor is the expectation on the part of many of those companies that the free trade agreement will be passed. I would suggest that they should not be so certain about that, but the expectation has led them in a number of cases to design at this stage to shift production to the U.S. That would seem to have been the case with Cross-LaSalle and the recent Hawker-Siddley shut-down. It is possible, given that Birla produces in the U.S. as well, that this was a factor in that shut-down.
The third factor has been confirmed for us by the Federal Business Development Bank with respect to Birla Industries. They and the management of the company, in their statement about the shut-down, pointed to the 10 cent increase over the past year in the value of the Canadian dollar. I think that appreciation is part of a quiet agreement between the Government and the U.S. Government with respect to the trade agreement, and it has resulted in this particular plant shutdown. It has also resulted in the shut-down of certain other auto parts producers across Ontario.
I have a sense that the Government does not understand what it is doing when it puts into effect a high interest rate policy which creates this tremendous increase in the value of the dollar. These high interest rates have now brought us to a point where the prime lending rate is 10.25 per cent at the chartered banks. That means a flow into this country of shortterm capital which does not go into new industries or new production but into speculative paper investments. At the same time we have an increase in the value of our dollar which, in the case of Birla Industries, has cost 152 people their jobs. Again, I think this is a sign of the lack of serious economic thinking and economic policy making on the part of the Government.

Mr. Speaker, the CBC Commentary program of February 3 featured comments by Dr. Peter Cole, regional health officer for the County of Peel, Ontario, who made the false statement that the abortion rate in the U.S. decreased after abortion on demand became legal in 1973. Dr. Cole misled the Canadian public by distorting the true facts, that abortion has indeed increased drastically since 1973.
The CBC showed its bias by not even having one pro-life commentator on the program despite the fact that a substantial number of people stand on both sides of the question. The question that begs to be answered is how the CBC Commentary guests are selected, and by whom. As well, why was the pro-life side of the issue not presented after the Supreme Court decision on the Morgentaler case?
This is another example of the CBC once again doing a poor job in keeping bias out of its programs. It is hoped that the ongoing investigation by the CRTC will censor the CBC and force it to curtail its biased programming and henceforth give equal opportunity for both sides of all issues to be heard, and not just what the CBC wants people to hear.

Mr. Speaker, the chief, the council, and the Spallumcheen Indian Band members reject the Minister of Indian Affairs' (Mr. McKnight) recent proposed child welfare program. They reject not only the policy but also the so-called consultation process. They believe that by transferring jurisdiction over native children's welfare to provincial Governments the federal Government is actually breaching its trust responsibility for Indian people and is playing politics with the lives of Indian children.
Seven years ago this band began its own child welfare program based on a thoughtful and well developed band bylaw which gave the band members the right to administer their own child welfare programs, which they have done exceptionally well. They do not wish now to surrender this jurisdiction to provincial Governments.
If native self-government is to be a reality in Canada, those bands which presently have complete jurisdiction and responsibility over their child welfare programs must be able to continue to act in that fashion.

Mr. Speaker, Quebecers and Canadians learned yesterday of the death of one of the most important figures in Canadian theatre, Jean Gascon. Jean Gascon, actor and producer, distinguished himself as cofounder and director of the Theatre du Nouveau Monde, founder of the National Theatre School in Montreal, artistic director of the Stratford Theatre in Ontario and, in 1977, director of the National Arts Centre in Ottawa.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to pay a personal tribute to Mr. Gascon and say how important he was in discovering and establishing the theatre in Quebec to people of my generation. Jean Gascon helped us discover and love Moliere. He gave us the desire to go to the theatre and pride in seeing local Canadian actors perform on our stages in Quebec. He gave us a taste for quality. With Denise Pelletier and Jean-Louis Roux, he made us realize that the theatre was as important in our lives as science and the other professions.
To his family and to all theatre people, I offer my sincerest condolences on behalf of Quebecers and Canadians; we all share their sorrow.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has lost one of its most prominent performing artists. The founder of the Theatre du Nouveau Monde and the father of modern theatre in Quebec became one of the most respected figures in this country.
His work as actor, producer and director took him from Montreal to Paris. Subsequently, he was made artistic director of the well-known Stratford Festival. His passion for the theatre was overwhelming: From Tennessee Williams to Tchekov, Moliere, Claudel and Shakespeare, he made us laugh and cry.

CANADA-FRANCE DISPUTE-STATUS OF ST. PIERRE AND MIQUELON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the papers are full of reports of the cod war between Canada and the United States, and the posturing politicians vying for the presidential prize in Paris are talking about the situation. Mitterand says it is "an unacceptable situation". Mr. Chirac says it is "an absurd conflict". I fundamentally agree with them both, Mr. Speaker, but not for the reasons they say.
I suggest it is time that the last of the empires on North American soil came to an end. The Spanish left several hundred years ago, the British have gone, and now it is time that the French got out of North American affairs.

April 22, 1988
Discussions with France should not be just on fish but also on this anachronism of history. St. Pierre and Miquelon should no longer be a curiosity clone of France but should take its proper territorial place and develop a status with Canada.
As a former colony, which found its national soul, Canada knows what independence is all about. It is time that St. Pierre and Miquelon cast aside the shackles of history, came out of the shadow of Napoleon, and entered the 20th century.
If France still stays imperial on fish, then it better get realistic in its relations with Canada. Why should we buy the French airbus or submarine if we cannot agree on basic cod?
The Canadian union is all embracing, and if Newfoundland can join the union and sustain its national distinct character, so can St. Pierre and Miquelon. Viva St. Pierre and Miquelon libre! Vive St. Pierre and Miquelon Canadien!

ETHANOL ADVOCATED FOR USE IN AUTOMOBILES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by the end of 1992 all Canadian car owners will be driving automobiles powered by unleaded gasoline. Manufacturers will thus be in need of a good octane enhancer. Ethanol, an alcohol based fuel derived from agricultural sources, is just what the refineries need.
In spite of the proven ability of this product to fulfil Canadian fuel needs and at the same time help farmers by converting their lower quality feed grains into fuel, the tariff provisions in the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal favour the choice of a petrochemical octane enhancer over ethanol. As well, Canada's own Petro-Canada has been very negative about ethanol and has even refused to blend the product at its refinery in Taylor, B.C. Why does its shareholder, the Government of Canada, not instruct Petro-Canada to reconsider?
1 urge the Minister to begin promoting ethanol for use in all Canadian cars by 1992 to avoid lead pollution and to enhance the agricultural sector.

speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Acting Prime Minister. Following the Prime Minister's first summit with President Reagan in March of 1985, he said he had a deal on acid rain. He said the same thing following his summits of 1986 and 1987. However, to the great regret of all Canadians, the United States has not cut acid rain by one drop since the Prime Minister has taken office, despite all these great deals.
Now, the leading private environmental agency in the world, the Sierra Club, has said: "Mulroney is doing his own country a great disservice".
The Prime Minister is having his fourth and final summit with President Reagan next week. Will the President and the Prime Minister be signing a meaningful treaty to actually cut emissions of acid rain from the United States, or will this just be another summit full of photo opportunities and talk and no real action to cut acid rain?

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S FORTHCOMING MEETING WITH UNITED STATES PRESIDENT

Member will know that this Government and the Prime Minister have given the highest possible priority, to the question of making progress on acid rain. Member would quote a publication suggesting that it is somehow against Canada's interests for the Prime Minister of Canada to make the fight against acid rain an international priority and for him and for his Government to assume leadership at home in Canada so that we can ensure that we go with our hands clean into those negotiations and discussions with the United States.
This Government has acted very vigorously to deal with the threat of acid rain to Canada. We have not had the success that we have been seeking. We continue to seek that kind of movement.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: COST OF DAMAGE CAUSED BY ACID RAIN-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:

We have made considerable progress. We have made more progress than the previous government, because we have consistently set a high priority on the acid rain issue. We have not attained our objectives, but we intend to continue to seek further progress.

The Hon. Member talks about whether or not we will be presenting a bill to the United States. That proposal was put forward by his colleague, the Liberal Party spokesman on the environment, some time ago. It is a classic example of a stunt: when you have no policy, you pursue a stunt. We have a policy, we have a goal. It is to reduce acid rain emissions in this country, and it is to reach an agreement with the United States. We are not interested in Liberal stunts.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-118, an Act to establish the Canadian International Trade Tribunal. 1 would first like to outline the main points of the Bill and the main concerns my Party has with it.
The Bill is something with which my Party is generally in agreement. It combines three existing agencies, the Canadian Import Tribunal, the Tariff Board, and the Textile and Clothing Board. It is the last board with which I have had the most association on account of the presence in Spadina of a very large textile and clothing industry. The duties and functions of the new tribunal are, first, to inquire and report on economic trade or commercial matters as requested by the Government. I will come back to that because that is a limitation on the powers presently available to the Textile and Clothing Board, a very grave limitation.
Second, it has the duty to inquire and report to the Minister of Finance on any tariff-related matter, including Canada's international rights and obligations. The Government will set the terms of reference for those two inquiry functions. In addition to its research functions, the new tribunal will take over the existing appeal function of the Tariff Board. It will hear appeals of Revenue Canada decisions regarding customs and excise duties and classifications.
Finally, the tribunal will provide direct access on injury inquiries. When a Canadian industry considers that it has been injured it will have direct access to the board. We are particularly in favour of that aspect of its functions.
At present the Textile and Clothing Board provides the right of direct access for an injury inquiry upon petition by producers. That is to say, if clothing or textile producers feel they are being injured by imports or subsidies in a foreign country, they have the right to petition directly to the Textile and Clothing Board. That right is now to be extended to other industries, and we are in favour of that.
The new tribunal will then examine whether the increased imports are the primary cause of the injury. Obviously there could be loss of business for reasons other than imports, even if imports were also present. Therefore, it will examine whether the imports are the primary cause of the injury. However, it cannot deal with subsidized and anti-dumping conditions for injury inquiries.
I am very concerned that it will not be able to deal with subsidies. The matter of subsidies has been a very important

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak on Bill C-118 for a brief period of time. It is noted that this Bill introduces amendments to the customs tariff in response to a request from the private sector. Duties are being removed on a range of equipment used by the oilsands industry, such as certain differentials, compressors for motor vehicles, steel rods for farm silos, recording tapes used to make cassettes for the blind, certain model kits, and burial shrouds. The Bill also provides for a few technical amendments to the customs tariff.
It is, as others have remarked, not a big Bill. We can compare this Bill to C-87. Bill C-87 concerned the development and implementation of a new harmonized system. A great deal of work was done on tariffs and so on. Much of what was of concern to manufacturers, importers and other business people was satisfied in that legislation. In any case, as one of the Parliamentary Secretaries to the Deputy Prime Minister and the President of the Privy Council noted, most people are preoccupied with the free trade agreement that has been negotiated with the United States. We are waiting to see what the Government will do with legislation to implement the agreement. We are waiting also to see what will happen in the United States on that agreement and what its impact will be on the Trade Bill now being considered in Congress as well as other activities that must occur in the United States in that regard.
One of the elements of the free trade agreement that concerns us all is what it may mean to the future economic development in our country. We have a reputation for selling off our vast resources to other countries to the profit of those who own companies involved in shipping our wood, minerals,
Customs Tariff
fish, coal and oil which produce jobs. The primary motivation of the Americans, is to ensure the availability of just those resources that we have. Of course, the old pattern of selling off our resources to Japan, Europe, the United States or Great Britain so jobs can be produced elsewhere rather than in Canada has, over the years, inescapably led to a never tested, rather casual, happy economic existence for this country because we did not take a close look at the real world. It is wrong that those same elements in our society and in the United States which sold off our resources cheaply so jobs could be produced elsewhere will be able by this agreement to ensure that that state of affairs continues in Canada.
There is a lesson in the contents of this Bill which refers to a number of items. Let me just list a few as they are listed in the schedule attached. Other Members have made reference to this list, but let me do it again. First, with respect to the removal of tariffs, these include those on specified machinery used by the oil sands production industry, certain compressors and differentials for automotive vehicles, steel rods used in the construction of silos, unrecorded magnetic tapes used to make cassettes for the blind, certain model kits and burial shrouds.
Mr. Speaker and colleagues in this House, does it not strike you as being a little ridiculous that Canada does not manufacture burial shrouds, much less the electronic technology and construction equipment and equipment for the oil sands industry? Does it not strike you as ironic that we do not produce these things in a country in which these products are commonly used? That calls attention to our continuing problem. We have got into a mind-set by which we are willing to depend upon others to use our resources to produce products which are sold back to us. We have not even developed the capacity to produce products which have a vast market in Canada. If we are not capable of making implements for the mining and petroleum industry ourselves and capable of doing so well that the machinery and implements can be sold elsewhere, then we are failing our own country and our own people. It is for this reason that the free trade agreement is an admission of failure.
At least perhaps it is a failure that results from a marriage of attitudes between this Government and that of the United States because the Americans believe that Canada should remain one vast resource pool for the benefit of others. If there is any doubt that that is not the case, one need only look at the free trade agreement.
If one thing is clear, the free trade agreement deprives us of the mechanisms by which we can mobilize our own capacities and industries to produce jobs here with respect particularly to science and technology. We should embark seriously on an effort to make this a knowledge-based economy, but we have put ourselves in a situation by the conditions accepted in the free trade agreement with respect to control of our industries in the face of foreign acquisition from the United States that we cannot mobilize the kind of scientific and research thrust necessary to depart from this long-standing habit of great

enrichment of the few at the expense of the many who could have jobs generated from those resources.
Let us just consider, in discussing this small Bill but nevertheless symbolic Bill, some of the things that we would not have been able to do if a century ago we had this free trade agreement with the United States. Every one of the following would have been impossible under this free trade agreement: prairie settlement, the Canadian Pacific Railway, our domestic steel industry, the Canadian National Railway, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, Air Canada, the Canadian Wheat Board, de Havilland, Canadair, Petro-Canada, health insurance, the Auto Pact, Bell Canada, Northern Telecom, Hydro Quebec, the James Bay Development, Lavalin and, indeed, the domestic automobile industry.
All of these areas in which Canada has had success which have benefited Canadians and created jobs-all things which Canadians hold dear as the manifestation of what we are capable of and on which we are prepared to take government action in co-operation with industry-would be impossible to do again under this free trade agreement.
That is what is at issue, not elimination of tariffs but the elimination of the capacity in Canada to organize our resources, our manpower, our industry and our inventiveness to ensure that in this sovereign nation we can move forward to a new kind of vision of a prosperous yet just land which would be a symbol for all the world and a certain contrast to the neighbour with whom we are going to sign this agreement.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Windsor- Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) has expressed himself more than once on the subject of development and the need to develop our industries. He has just listed industries which could not have been developed had the proposed trade deal agreement been in place in the past.
I know he is also concerned, for example, in the future, the not too distant future, for the development of energy from hydrogen. I have heard him comment on this subject, and I am wondering whether he can comment on the relationship of the trade deal restrictions to our chances for developing the potential that we have for the hydrogen energy system in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to answer that very briefly. Of course, the many reports that have advocated, as we have advocated, a national mission for Canada in hydrogen technology have pointed out that it is not possible to embark on such a mission without it being owned by Canadians. There is no question that this mission would require participation by the Government. Unquestionably, it would involve in some measure, for example, subsidies and procurement largely limited to Canadian interests. It would have to involve the ownership of those companies which are participants.
According to the free trade agreement, we could not insist upon a research and development standard to be met after the acquisition of Canadian companies. In brief, if Canada is to launch into a future which would be defined in terms of the knowledge we possess and the technology we have developed, one way of doing that would be to have a large mission which is uniquely national. It is not to be a hanger-on, a follower or a passenger, a participant in someone else's national mission, as is the case with the space station. However valuable that may be, it does not have the mobilizing characteristics that bring people together with pride to point to a vision of Canada which this kind of technology would produce for us, using the resources and skills we already have and the technology we have already developed to some extent.
If we are to go on such a mission, that mission must be owned by Canada totally. That would be specifically excluded by the free trade agreement. That mission is very much like Northern Telecom, Canadair, de Havilland, CP and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, institutions and corporations which have been established in the Canadian interest. They were established because we felt it necessary to establish the means by which we could maintain our uniqueness, our sovereignty and particularly our economic sovereignty.

Debate.
Canadian International Trade Tribunal

Mr. Speaker, I am glad that I do have this chance to speak on this Bill, Bill C-110. The point that I wish to make in this Bill is that while we support it because we support the idea, the general principle of bringing the three boards together into one, that is, the Canadian Import Tribunal, the Tariff Board and the Textile and Clothing Board, we are concerned that the powers are too limited and that powers that did belong to the Textile and Clothing Board will be taken away in the new legislation.
The powers being proposed here are that they inquire and report on economic trade or commercial matters as requested by the Government, that they inquire into and report to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on any tariff-related matter including Canada's international rights and obligations, and on those two inquiries, they will of course be directed by the Government's terms of reference. In addition, the tribunal will take over the existing appeal functions of the Tariff Board. That is to say, it will hear appeals of Revenue Canada decisions about customs and excise duties and classifications.
Then, fourth, it will provide direct access on injury inquiries. This is the one that concerns me very much. The existing right of the Textile and Clothing Board for an injury inquiry upon direct petition by producers will be extended to all industries. We are very much in favour of that. However, when the new tribunal examines whether increased imports are the primary cause of injury, they will not be able to deal with subsidizing and anti-dumping concerns. This is a very serious restriction and I think it is very unfortunate.
I want to explain why I think it is so unfortunate by giving an example of what has recently come to my attention through the clothing industry in Spadina. From talking with some of the representatives of the corporations that produce clothing in Spadina, and through Style magazine, I find that there is a new player in the field. Thailand has, in the last two or three years, moved from a country whose main export was rice to a country whose main export is clothing.
Thailand has a large and fairly modern clothing industry financed jointly with countries such as Japan, Hong Kong, Taiwan, and the United Kingdom. There are over 400,000 workers in their clothing industry, move than twice as many as we have in Canada. Their population, of course, is twice as large as ours. Last year they exported 140 million pieces of clothing, one-quarter of their total national production.
According to reports handed out by the Thai Government, their export is increasing at 23 per cent per annum. In the past year they sent only two or three per cent of their total production to Canada but they wish to increase that very considerably.
It is also alleged, although of course not reported in their government hand-out, that their labour conditions are very substandard, that there is very serious suppression of the rights of trade unionists in that country, and that large numbers of

April 22, 1988
Canadian International Trade Tribunal
the workers, young women largely from the countryside, are required to live a regimented life in dormitories on low wages. It is also alleged that quite young children are used as labour there.
These practices have been excluded from accepted labour practices in Canada, Great Britain, and western Europe. Therefore, we should not be encouraging countries which use these unacceptable practices to produce goods at prices below world market prices for the sake of competition. That is unfair competition.
Unfortunately, it is quite possible that that situation would be removed from the jurisdiction of the Textile and Clothing board and the new tribunal to be created. It is not a matter included in their jurisdiction according to the description which we have been given of this Bill. In particular, subsidies and related matters are excluded. I believe, also, that labour conditions would no longer be considered.
I want to point in particular to a very aggressive subsidy policy of the Government of Thailand. It is the policy to promote producers of garments for export and to give them heavy tax privileges. That is to say, the producers of export clothing will pay a lower rate of tax than will producers of clothing for domestic use. The industry ministry has also exempted garment factories that have no more than 20 sewing machines from the requirement of obtaining a permit for setting up a factory. There are also tax rebates given to exporters who use local raw materials. For imported raw materials the duty on the manufacture of garments for export is refundable. There is also an export tax and business tax exemption for manufacturers of garments for export.
These are very weighty exemption privileges and are subsidies which the new board will not be allowed to examine. Another even more direct form of subsidy is a rebate on electricity payments to manufacturers of garments for export.
I hope that this will be considered very seriously by the Government because Canadian producers will not be able to come before this new tribunal, which will unify the present three tribunals, to raise issues such as this very recent issue with regard to Thailand. It is only this year that some Canadian producers became fully aware of these conditions in Thailand. It would be unfortunate if the Government introduced legislation which would reduce or perhaps cut off their ability to take the matter up with the new tribunal.
There are other difficulties with this new tribunal. It offers very little protection to small and medium-sized producers unless they can organize in large associations because the tribunal can only take up an injury complaint if the producers of the majority of goods petition for the injury inquiry. However, within the garment industry there are so many subsectors and sub-subsectors which have very specific conditions of their own and which relate very specifically to other countries, either for export or for import, that it is not at all clear that this requirement of having a majority of the
producers of the goods in question petition would be interpreted in a way which would be properly sensitive to the needs of producers in some of the sectors.
In Spadina in particular we have many factories with 10, 20, 30, or 40 employees. These are long-standing, traditional firms for the most part. They are not mass organizations. They have been a very important part of the life of Canada, both in the production of clothing and in the life of the City of Toronto and of Spadina in particular. They are the mainstay of many families, including many immigrant families for whom that is often the first and best opportunity of employment.
In fact, I have talked with immigrants who are themselves from Asia who are not happy at the thought that their jobs may be transferred back to Asia from where they came. They came here as legitimate immigrants seeking, as has been said over the decades, a better life. They met the conditions and arrived. They have settled in Canada and do not like to see the better life being exported to some other country, even to the country from which they came.
The new tribunal must be reshaped to enlarge its scope so that it can take account of things like the alleged very bad labour conditions, and either the bad labour laws or the neglect of labour laws in countries like Thailand. It must also take account of the subsidies which have not been quantified. We do not know the number of dollars or the per cent of costs concerned. However, with regard to the tax exemptions and the rebates for electrical power consumed, it looks like a very considerable subsidy, particularly since the Thai Government reports that labour costs as a share of the total are increasing and that costs other than labour and raw materials are increasing as compared to raw materials.
They have a legitimate natural advantage in raw materials because of their climate. They can produce fabrics such as cotton that we cannot. That is fair enough for them to use that, but it is not fair for them to use bad labour conditions or direct subsidies apart from what is allowable under the GATT.
Therefore, we do need a broader tribunal to be able to give the producers in Canada, who understand the situation, the chance to bring this information to the attention of the tribunal. The tribunal should not only have the jurisdiction to inquire but also have the jurisdiction to make recommendations. Who better than a tribunal, such as the present Clothing and Textile Board, can recognize the facts, the conditions and the standards by which recommendations ought to be made?
Of course, it is still up to the Minister, having received recommendations, to take action as he or she sees fit. But I think it is very unfortunate to remove from this board the power and the duty that the present Textile and Clothing Board has, the power and duty to make recommendations in cases of injury by imports. Therefore, I hope the Government will take these matters into consideration before the Bill has been finalized.
April 22, 1988

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak on this Bill today since I did not have the opportunity to do so on previous occasions. I understand that some Members would want to amend certain sections of the Bill about which I am concerned myself. For example, according to the definition in section 2(g) of the Bill, "employer" includes:
a Member of Parliament who, in that capacity, employs or engages the services of any person or has the direction and control of staff employed by or engaged to provide research or associated services to the caucus members of a political party represented in Parliament.
Further on in the Bill, it says in paragraph 3(3):
Notwithstanding sub-section (1), an employee may, because of the nature of the employee's duties, be required by an employer-in other words, the Member of Parliament described in Clause 2 may be required by an employer, by me, the Member for Gatineau-to perform his or her duties from time to time in a designated smoking room.
In fact, according to this Bill I should tell my office staff that if they want to smoke, I can require them to go and work in a room I would set aside as the designated smoking room in my office. I have a problem with this, because first of all, Mr. Speaker, in our office we work as a team and we respect each other. For instance, we have job descriptions, something that is not required by Parliament. However, I went through this exercise because I respect my employees and I want them to have a say in their working conditions, and I want those working conditions to be respected. I have to be able to negotiate these working conditions with my employees, including whether or not they are allowed to smoke and whether or not they want to smoke in the office. This Bill would deny me the right to sit down with my employees and discuss whether they want to restrict smoking in the office. In that case, the Bill is a threat, not only to the freedom of my employees but also to my own freedom as an employer to create in my office an atmosphere where we work as a team and respect each other's freedom. That is why I have a problem with this Bill.
Now, someone might say to me, "Well, yes, it is only a paragraph and we could exclude all MPs' offices; that would solve the problem." No, Mr. Speaker, that would not solve the problem because I feel that if a bill were to exclude MPs, it would not be fair for me to rise in the House and support a bill that excludes me, that gives me freedoms that I would not allow, for example, to the library staff, to the committee staff, to civil servants in general, etc., namely all those covered by this Bill. I find that would be unfair.
Non-smokers' Health Act
So it shows the flaws that exist in this Bill, unfortunately. We must deal with the problem, this very important problem of smoke, which affects those around the smoker, it has been pointed out, and solve it.
But unfortunately, this Bill goes further. To solve a health problem, it will create legal problems, it will create problems for working conditions and employee-employer relations. It will also disturb the very special atmosphere that develops in an MP's office, where all the staff must work as a team to serve the constituents who elected us, their Members of Parliament, to serve them not only at some hours of the day, but to be available and to be ready to meet their needs at any time. We all have emergency answering services so that when our constituents call our offices, they do not go unanswered.
So I could not tell a constituent that he or she cannot speak to a certain member of my staff because that person is then in the smoking lounge. That would bother me a lot. I would prefer to continue running our offices with respect for our employees.
I understand very well that the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) does not appreciate that I refer to the respect for employees, because she finds it very difficult to respect anyone, including herself. But I insist just the same, Mr. Speaker, that a legislation that would be enacted by the House, by elected representatives who must at all times meet the needs of the Canadian people, should not include provisions that affect the service we may offer our constituents, that might affect the atmosphere and work conditions, the spirit of co-operation that must and does exist in our offices, Mr. Speaker. Otherwise we could not serve our constituents.
Therefore, I would suggest that we continue with the Government's legislation, which itself raises some problems, but I believe it certainly would be easier to iron out those problems than the ones which are so evident in this legislation.
Mr. Speaker, indeed I find that this Bill very well reflects a certain philosophy that is apparent in every question raised by the Hon. Member, a tone of authority that calls for unquestioned obedience. When she wants to solve a problem, she throws a very wide net that will create other problems while attempting to solve the problem at hand. I believe this is evident in the wording of the legislation, especially the clause I read earlier: "An employee may, because of the nature of the employee's duties, be required by an employer to perform his or her duties from time to time in a designated smoking room."
This means a "designated smoking room" could be a small box no larger than this, and I would have to tell my legislative assistant, who is now looking at the Abortion Act, a very, very sensitive subject Mr. Speaker, who is preparing a very sensible document on the matter and who suddenly would want to smoke, relax a bit because he works long hours, he works over weekends and all that on very sensitive matters, I would have to tell him: You cannot relax now, or then you will have to go to the smoking room to continue your work because I cannot

April 22, 1988
Non-smokers' Health Act
afford that you stop for 15 ou 20 minutes since the legislation must be ready.
So, we must face reality. We must tell that person to take with him or her all the big books and the Statutes of Canada- because somebody working on legislation like the new abortion law must do very extensive research in very big books-and go right away to the designated area and stay there as long as he or she wants to smoke. One must admit that those 35,000 deaths if we are to believe experts, is quite a high price to pay and for two reasons. First, it means that we lose a segment of our population, often the most active one, at an age where it could achieve a lot for the country. And second the use of tobacco is very costly for our health care system and it accounts for an enormous part of our medical expenses.
Costs are also incurred as a result for example of fires either in our communities or in our forests and so on and also as a result of traffic accidents. When will we know the exact number of accidents caused by someone who dropped or lighted a cigarette while driving?
So all these costs are difficult to assess, but nonetheless they are important costs.
There is also a cost attached to non-smokers environment. Those who decided to quit smoking at some point in their life are innocent victims of smokers. That is also a cost.
The physical well being of people can be a cost. I was a smoker for some time and since I quit, I think I am in a better physical condition, which enables me to be more of a fighter in the House of Commons, or at least to have a very positive attitude towards what the socialists say. If I was less fit, I
would be less able to defend our country against socialist policies, if we can describe them as such.
Furthermore, smoking reduces productivity. People working in an office who smoke ... It is unfortunate to have to say that, Mr. Speaker, to the leader of the socialist party who secretly smokes cigars, Havana cigars, communist cigars he can afford because he lives in a wealthy country.
I beg my colleague to try and convince her leader to stop smoking. It is not nice. It is not nice either to develop secret policies. Her leader should perhaps emulate the leader of the Liberal Party: I hear he does not smoke. I am sure that the leader of my party does not. So, with that Bill, it will now be prohibited to use billboards to promote smoking and that prohibition would be in effect as of January 1991.
Second, advertisement at the place of business of a retailer will be prohibited as of January 1993. The value of the sponsoring agreements using the brand name of a tobacco product shall not exceed the level of support agreed to in 1987.
Most other types of advertising and promotion will be prohibited from January 1st 1988 onward. Warnings on the health effects of tobacco and information on its toxic constituents must be printed on cigarette packages.
There is also a provision to require that health warnings be put inside packages. Finally, according to existing legislation and consultative process, various measures are already in effect to limit tobacco use to smoking rooms or areas, or to prohibit smoking in certain places.
I also want to mention the policies of this Government, including the Treasury Board policy that limits tobacco use to certain areas since October 1st, 1987. Aside from a few exceptions, it will be forbidden to smoke in all Public Service offices beginning January 1st, 1989. I hope that those rules will also apply to the socialist leader who likes to sneak a smoke. I hope that he will abide by Public Service rules, that he will object to the importation of cigars from communist countries, namely Cuba, for which he pays with capitalist money, Mr. Speaker.

Indeed, the fewer possible smokers there are in this country, the better it is for the health of all Canadians. As a former smoker, Mr. Speaker, I know. I stopped smoking seven years ago and now I feel much better physically. To stop smoking is a very positive step for Canadian men and women to take and to those who have never smoked, 1 say: Hear hear! Getting back to Bill C-204, Section 3 reads as follows:
Every employer shall provide a smoke-free environment where all employees
may perform the duties that are directly or indirectly related to their

How are we to define, in this case, the term "smoke-free"? Are we only talking about smoke? If there is a smoking room on one floor, will absolutely all the smoke generated in that room stay there? Can we be sure that some of that smoke will not spread through the building or into adjacent offices? Have we set up systems or devices to check constantly and systematically the quantity of smoke in the air? Is there an alarm system which will trigger a buzzer or start a fan when a particular level of smoke in the air is reached or exceeded?
And, Mr. Speaker, when we are talking about the House of Commons and Members' offices where a designated smoking room is provided, I wonder, if I understand correctly the purpose of this Bill, whether this will not be extended to our riding offices, because they are, after all, an extension of the offices of Members of the House of Commons. Considering that a riding office is often far less spacious than an office in one of the departments here in Ottawa or in the Parliament Buildings, how can we provide a smoking room inside a riding office? Will we have to rent another building or rent space in the building next door if we don't have enough room? Will we have to find another space and let our employees go there when they want to smoke during the day?
Mr. Speaker, I realize our Government is concerned about the health of Canadians, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has, through Bill C-51, launched a national anti-smoking program, headed by representatives of the federal and provincial Governments and our national health care agencies. Mr. Speaker, I will speak on Motion Nos. 1 and 2 before us at report stage. I will preface this with the remark that if there are two Members of this House who are more guilty of speaking on and on and on whenever the occasion arises, it is the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) and the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria). These two Members go on and on and on at all times when the Government is trying to get through very important legislation critical to the well-being of Canada. For them to say on this occasion that anyone who wants to speak at report stage or third reading of this particular Bill is somehow frustrating the great wishes of Canada, I cannot understand that rationale whatsoever.
I wish that the hon. proposer of the motions with which we are dealing, namely, Motion Nos. 1 and 2, had taken some time to explain what these amendments are all about. The Member brushed them off as mere technicalities. It took me considerable time to read through them, referring backward and forward to the Bill to find out exactly what they were about. The first one is to add words in the definition section. In talking about designated smoking rooms, it said initially that a designated smoking room means (a) for an office building constructed prior to January, 1990, an enclosed space" et cetera. Now we have added the words "for an office building or other enclosed work space". I guess that is a necessary amendment if you read it in reference to Clause 4 of the Bill, to which I will speak a little later.
When we start telling people what they can do, where, and where they cannot do a certain thing we get ourselves into trouble and problems start to arise. What exactly is meant by an enclosed work space? I think we all understand what we mean by an office. But what do we mean by an enclosed work space? A workshop would obviously be one. Whether you would want to ban smoking in all workshops, I do not know. But there are the marginal cases.
April 22, 1988

During this winter, Mr. Speaker, you as well as other Members must have seen the stone masons who work on the Parliament Buildings. These are people who would obviously be covered by this Bill. During the summer they can work outside and presumably they would be able to smoke as much they wanted as they work on Parliament's stone work. In winter when the temperatures are a little colder and the weather sometimes inclement, a structure is erected made of scaffolding and two-by-fours. It is enclosed with plywood or canvas. The stone masons work in what might be described under this Bill, were it to become law, as an enclosed work space. This illustrates the difficulties we get into when we try to be so precise. I do not think that I would want to tell a stone mason, who is legally smoking at his work in June or July, that he should not be able to smoke when doing the same work in October or November. That deals with the amendments contemplated in Motion No. 1.
I understand that Motion No. 2 is being dealt with at the same time and I have a few comments with respect to Motion No. 2, which seeks to amend Clause 4. This would add the word "enclosed" between the words "other" and "work". The present clause reads "No person shall smoke in any office or other work space provided by an employer, outside of the designated smoking room or designated smoking area". I am certainly in favour of this proposed amendment, Mr. Speaker, because, of course, work space could be, unless you add that adjective, an open field. Surely it was not the intention, even of the Hon. Member from Broadview-Greenwood, to stop people working in the fields of the Experimental Farm from smoking. I do not think that was the case at all. I am entirely in favour of adding the word "enclosed" before work space in Clause No. 4.
In discussing this matter there is one other point I want to make. It is an important point because it has constitutional implications for the part of the country that I represent.
You, Sir, are undoubtedly aware of a court ruling made several years ago that said that a municipal undertaking in the Northwest Territories was to be designated as an undertaking or business under the definition of Section 2 of the Canada Labour Code. There is a long story behind this as to why it came about, but for certain reasons under the Canada Labour Code municipal operations within the Territories were deemed to be federal work or a federal undertaking. Of course, this Bill would apply, pursuant to paragraph 2(c), to all federal works and undertakings. Therefore, because of that court ruling it would presumably apply to municipal undertakings in the Northwest Territories. I think if this Bill became law we would have to look at a further amendment to restrict that.
I do not think it is correct that we should legislate here with respect to whether somebody can smoke in a municipal garage in Fort Smith. There may be good arguments as to whether somebody should be allowed to smoke there or not, but it is not really the duty or the responsibility of the Parliament of Canada to say so. It would obviously be something which should be done by municipal by-law. Those are some of the
Non-smokers' Health Act
concerns that I have with the first two motions put before us today at the report stage debate.
